results.title: Designing for iPadOS — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple's platform-scoped design page for iPad. Covers the whole Apple side of items 1–3 in one place: layout adaptivity across orientations and window sizes, multitasking (Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager) and the expectation that the app is usable at any window size it can be given, plus pointer and external-keyboard support as first-class iPad input. This is the canonical entry point when arguing that an iPad app is not a stretched iPhone layout.

results.title: Layout — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for Apple's size class system (compact/regular horizontal and vertical) and the size-class-per-device/orientation table. States the guidance that you use horizontal and vertical size classes to specialize how much detail the interface shows, rather than keying off device model — the direct answer to 'what does Apple publish instead of CSS breakpoints.' Also covers safe areas, margins, and designing for varying window sizes.

results.title: Split views — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The named Apple alternative to a single stretched column: a split view managing multiple adjacent panes (sidebar, content list, detail), i.e. the two- and three-column NavigationSplitView pattern. Covers when to use a sidebar vs. a tab bar, collapse behavior when horizontal space becomes compact, and pane resizing — the mechanics that make a tablet layout genuinely tablet-shaped.

results.title: Pointing devices — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for iPadOS hybrid input: trackpad/mouse navigation alongside touch, and the named pointer effects (highlight, lift, hover) with guidance on which element sizes each suits — highlight as the default for bar buttons and tab bars, lift for medium elements with a background. Notes the iPadOS 26 change to a more precise pointer that no longer magnetizes or rubber-bands to targets. Establishes that pointer feedback is an enhancement layered on top of touch, not a requirement — the basis for 'hover must not be load-bearing.'

results.title: Building a desktop-class iPad app — Apple Developer Documentation
results.snippet: Apple's own framing of the iPad-app-as-desktop-app discipline: adopting desktop-class enhancements for multitasking with Stage Manager, document interactions, text editing, search, and navigation bar customization. This is the document that tells a designer what an iPad app must add once it can be windowed and resized arbitrarily under Stage Manager rather than owning the full screen.

results.title: Keyboards — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Covers the third leg of hybrid input: hardware/external keyboard support on iPad, keyboard shortcut conventions and discoverability, and how shortcuts should be organized rather than hidden. Relevant to item 3 (touch + pointer + keyboard simultaneously) and to the desktop half of the question where macOS and iPadOS shortcut conventions converge.

results.title: Use window size classes | Adaptive Apps | Android Developers
results.snippet: The authoritative dp breakpoint table the question asks for. Width: compact <600dp, medium 600–839dp, expanded 840–1199dp, large 1200–1599dp, extra-large >=1600dp (large/extra-large added for desktop and connected displays). Height: compact <480dp, medium 480–899dp, expanded >=900dp. Each class is tied to device-population percentages (e.g. medium width covers 93.73% of tablets in portrait) and to a layout recommendation: single pane at compact, canonical layouts (list-detail, supporting pane) from medium/expanded up. Also states that width alone is usually sufficient, with height mattering for the medium-width/compact-height landscape edge case where two panes are impractical — directly the 'stretched phone layout fails' argument in Google's own words.

results.title: Applying layout — window size classes | Material Design 3
results.snippet: Material's own primary statement of the breakpoint system (M3 now calls these 'breakpoints', formerly window size classes): opinionated window sizes at which layout changes to match available space, device conventions, and ergonomics. Pairs each breakpoint with the navigation component and pane count Material prescribes — navigation bar + single pane at compact, navigation rail + single pane at medium (600–839dp), rail or drawer + multi-pane at expanded (840–1199dp). This is the design-side counterpart to the Android developer breakpoint table and the source a designer, not an engineer, should cite.

results.title: Canonical layouts | Material Design 3
results.snippet: The named Material alternatives to a stretched phone layout: list-detail, supporting pane, and feed. Defines each as an expert-validated starting pattern and specifies the breakpoint behavior — list-detail shows list OR detail at compact/medium and both panes simultaneously at expanded width, with list selection driving the detail pane; supporting pane splits a primary display area from a secondary contextual area; feed adapts a grid from one scrolling column to a multi-column scrolling feed. Sub-pages exist per layout (e.g. /canonical-examples/list-detail).

results.title: Adaptive app quality guidelines | App quality | Android Developers
results.snippet: Google's stated large-screen quality tiers, by their current official names: Tier 3 Adaptive ready, Tier 2 Adaptive optimized, Tier 1 Adaptive differentiated. Tier 3 is the baseline entry point; Tier 2 requires responsive/adaptive layouts across all form factors; Tier 1 requires an experience impossible on a phone — convenient multitasking and drag and drop, plus support for foldable postures such as tabletop. This is the tiered checklist a designer is measured against, and it is the requirements document behind the multitasking and drag-and-drop parts of the original question. (Tier detail pages: /guide/topics/large-screens/tier-1-overview, /tier-2-overview.)

results.title: Navigation rail — guidelines | Material Design 3
results.snippet: Primary spec for the navigation rail, the component that replaces the phone's bottom navigation bar on tablets. States the rail is for switching between top-level views on mid-sized devices and is specifically for medium window widths of 600–839dp — a tablet or foldable in portrait — and that a single-pane layout is recommended at that breakpoint because width is still limited. Gives the exact numeric boundary at which a designer must swap navigation components rather than stretch the phone pattern.

results.title: Canonical layouts | Views | Android Developers
results.snippet: The Android developer-side treatment of the same three canonical layouts, useful because it translates the Material design patterns into concrete resource-qualifier and breakpoint implementation guidance (e.g. layout-w600dp) and states which layout suits which app type — list-detail for email/messaging collections, feed for news and social. Secondary to the m3.material.io pages for design intent, but it is the primary source for how the pattern is actually expressed at each dp threshold.

results.title: Keyboard accelerators - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: The single best primary source for the shortcut-divergence trap. Publishes an explicit "Common Keyboard Accelerators" table Microsoft says apps should be consistent with: Ctrl+Z undo, **Ctrl+Y redo** (macOS uses Cmd+Shift+Z), Ctrl+H search-and-replace, Ctrl+E begin editing, F2 rename (macOS uses Return), F5/Ctrl+R refresh, Ctrl+W close, Del/Ctrl+D delete, F6 / Shift+F6 to move between UI panes. Separates *control accelerators* (built into a control, fire only when it has focus) from *app accelerators* (global), and documents scoping via `ScopeOwner` so a context-menu Ctrl+C only fires inside its parent. Also states the localization landmine a web designer never hits: "in the Spanish version of Windows, Ctrl+N is used for bold instead of Ctrl+B" — accelerators must be localized from the predefined Virtual-Key set. Requires discoverability affordances: accelerators appended to tooltips automatically (`KeyboardAcceleratorPlacementMode`), shown inline in MenuFlyoutItem labels, and announced by Narrator via `AutomationProperties.AcceleratorKey`.

results.title: Windows app title bar - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: Microsoft's numeric spec for the window chrome a browser page has no concept of. Standard title bar height **32px** (grows to **48px** if you add a search box or person-picture), Mica default background, all title bar elements semi-transparent when the window is inactive, and colors must adapt to high-contrast themes via `SystemColors`. Behavioral requirements a naive custom title bar breaks: all empty/non-interactive space must be **draggable**; right-click or press-and-hold anywhere non-interactive must show the **system window menu**; double-click must toggle maximize/restore; single-click on the 16px window icon shows the system menu and double-click closes the window. Caption controls must use the exact Segoe Fluent glyphs (E921 ChromeMinimize, E922 ChromeMaximize, E923 ChromeRestore, E8BB ChromeClose), full-bleed backplates, and respond to rest/hover/pressed/active/inactive. Title may truncate with ellipsis but the icon and caption buttons must always stay fully visible; title text must respond to text-scaling, which may force the bar taller.

results.title: Support snap layouts for desktop apps on Windows 11 - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: The precise Electron/Tauri failure mode, named by Microsoft. Windows 11 shows the snap-layout flyout on hover over the maximize button (or Win+Z), but "if your app's main window has the maximize caption button available but does not show snap layouts, it may be because you've customized your caption buttons or title bar in a way that prevents it" — exactly what a web-tech app with an HTML title bar does. Fixes given: let the Windows App SDK windowing APIs draw the caption buttons, or for Win32 return `HTMAXBUTTON` from `WM_NCHITTEST` over your custom maximize button (code sample included); the page explicitly calls out Electron, saying to update to the v13 stable release to enable snap layouts. Also gives a hard resizing constraint web layouts routinely violate: minimum window width must be **at most 500 epx** to snap across common screen sizes, with **330 epx or less** recommended.

results.title: Commanding basics - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: Microsoft's taxonomy of *command surfaces* — the desktop concept responsive web design has no equivalent for. Enumerates where commands may live and when to use each: the app canvas (only for commands constantly needed for core scenarios; too many overwhelm and eat screen space), CommandBar (top, bottom, or both), **MenuBar** ("when the functionality in your app is too complex for a command bar" — the Windows analogue of the macOS menu bar, but drawn inside the app window, not a system-owned strip), and menus/context menus reached by right-click, which "save space by organizing commands and hiding them until the user needs them." Introduces **CommandBarFlyout** as the recommended contextual surface combining a command bar and a context menu with primary/secondary command tiers. Also states the direct-manipulation-first rule ("let users manipulate content directly rather than through commands that act on the content, such as dragging and dropping to rearrange list items") and the confirm-vs-undo policy: confirmation dialogs only for irreversible high-consequence actions, plain undo otherwise.

results.title: Access keys design guidelines - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: The Windows keyboard convention with **no macOS counterpart at all** — the clearest evidence that cross-platform keyboard parity is a myth. Access keys are Alt + one or more alphanumerics, pressed *sequentially* rather than simultaneously, with **KeyTips** — badges that appear over every access-key-bearing control the moment Alt is pressed. Documents scoping (Word's primary scope for ribbon tabs, secondary scope for the selected tab's commands) to cut cognitive load, and collision resolution: duplicates resolve to whichever element entered the visual tree first, and when "A", "A1", and "AB" coexist the single-character key wins and the rest are ignored. Selection guidance: prefer one character (which also auto-registers Alt+key as a shortcut), never more than two, avoid I/1 and O/0, follow Office precedent (F=File, H=Home), and fall back to a distinctive consonant or vowel when the first letter is taken ("N" for Insert, "W" for View). Access keys must be localized ("H" for Home in en-US, "I" for Inicio in es-ES) and are exposed to Narrator via AutomationProperties.AccessKey. KeyTip placement modes, offsets, and screen-edge auto-adjustment are specified.

results.title: Screen sizes and breakpoints for responsive design - Windows apps | Microsoft Learn
results.snippet: Windows' published breakpoint numbers, the third system alongside Apple size classes and Material window size classes: **Small up to 640px, Medium 641–1007px, Large 1008px and up**, mapped to TVs / tablets (7–12") / PCs, laptops, and Surface Hub (13"+). The critical desktop distinction from web media queries is stated outright: "design for the amount of screen space available to your app (the app's window), not the physical screen size" — a resizable, snappable window means the app can be at any breakpoint at any moment, which is the desktop analogue of iPadOS Split View. Breakpoints are measured in **effective pixels (epx)**, a viewing-distance-normalized unit, which is why a 1080p TV counts as Small (≈540 epx) while a 1080p monitor is Large. Sizes, margins, and positions must be multiples of **4 epx** so they land on whole pixels across the 100/125/150/175/200/225/250/300/350/400% scaling plateaus (text is exempt).

results.title: Custom Title Bar | Electron (official docs)
results.snippet: Primary framework doc for the window-chrome half of the native-feel gap. Documents `frame: false` frameless windows vs `titleBarStyle` (`hidden`, `hiddenInset`, `customButtonsOnHover`) which hides Electron's chrome while KEEPING the system's native window controls; `trafficLightPosition` for macOS traffic-light inset; and `titleBarOverlay` on Windows/Linux to put the caption buttons (minimize/maximize/close) back, with height, color and symbolColor options that default to system colors. Also covers the Window Controls Overlay CSS `env()` variables and `-webkit-app-region: drag` drag regions — the exact things a web designer omits, producing a page that cannot be moved or has controls colliding with app UI.

results.title: Menu | Electron (official API docs)
results.snippet: The menu-integration requirement in primary-source form, and it states the platform split a web design ignores: `Menu.setApplicationMenu` installs a single global menu bar on macOS, whereas on Windows/Linux the same menu is set as EACH window's top menu. Documents that Electron installs a default menu if the API is never called, that on macOS the first submenu always carries the app name (`appMenu` role), and enumerates the full `role` list — undo/redo/cut/copy/paste/selectAll, hide/hideOthers/unhide/quit, services, front/zoom/window, toggleTabBar/mergeAllWindows/moveTabToNewWindow, recentDocuments — i.e. the platform behaviors you get free by using roles and break by hand-rolling them. Notes that on macOS a role's `label` and `accelerator` are the only options honored, and that it is conventional to list open windows with a checkmark on the focused one.

results.title: Keyboard Shortcuts | Electron (official docs)
results.snippet: Directly answers 'platform keyboard conventions' for web-tech desktop apps. Covers the `accelerator` property on menu items as the correct way to bind shortcuts (so the binding is discoverable in the menu, not invisible), the `CmdOrCtrl` token that resolves the macOS-Cmd vs Windows-Ctrl divergence in one string, `globalShortcut` for system-wide bindings that fire when the app is unfocused, and `before-input-event` for shortcuts without a menu. This is the mechanism that fixes the most-cited Electron tell — web-style `keydown` handlers that fight the OS instead of registering as real accelerators.

results.title: Making Electron Apps Feel Native on Mac — Lotus (practitioner post-mortem)
results.snippet: The concrete native-feel checklist no platform vendor publishes, with working code per item. Twelve additions: show window only on `ready-to-show` (no white flash), persist and restore window position/size, explicit `-webkit-app-region` drag areas, system font at 14px rather than the web's 16px, `cursor: default` instead of `pointer` (a web tell), background color matched to dark mode to kill flashes, desaturated UI when the window is unfocused, a full standard macOS menu, accelerators attached to menu items, a real undo/redo stack, Preferences as a separate window on Cmd-comma rather than an in-app settings page, and offline support that queues actions and syncs on reconnect. Substantive engineering write-up, not SEO filler.

results.title: Window Customization | Tauri v2 (official docs)
results.snippet: The Tauri-side primary source and the clearest statement of the cost of faking window chrome in web tech: to build a custom titlebar you set `decorations: false` (config, `WebviewWindow.setDecorations`, or `WindowBuilder::decorations`) and then supply your own minimize/maximize/close markup — but on macOS this LOSES system-provided features such as window moving and snapping/alignment, so the doc recommends the transparent-titlebar-plus-window-background approach to keep native functions. Also covers size constraints, transparency, and the fact that macOS/Windows shadow and rounded-corner behavior is platform-specific rather than a CSS concern.

results.title: Context Menu | Electron (official docs)
results.snippet: Names a gap browser-based design never confronts: Electron ships NO built-in right-click context menu, so a web-technology app has none unless the developer builds one — you must listen for `context-menu` on the webContents and call `Menu.popup()` with the appropriate roles per target (text selection, image, link). Relevant to the original question's desktop-convention item on right-click menus: on the web the browser supplies one, in a shipped desktop app right-click does nothing by default, which is one of the most immediately legible 'this is a website in a window' symptoms.

results.title: The menu bar — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The single desktop convention with no web equivalent, stated primarily. Names the required menu order explicitly: "When present in the menu bar, the following menus appear in the order listed below. YourAppName (you supply a short version of your app's name for this menu's title), File, Edit, Format, View, App-specific menus, if any, Window, Help" — plus the Apple menu on the leading side and menu bar extras on the trailing side. Directives a web design omits entirely: "Support the default system-defined menus and their ordering"; "Always show the same set of menu items… If a menu bar item isn't actionable, disable the action instead of hiding it" (the opposite of the web habit of conditionally rendering nav). Also notes the system implements standard items for you (Edit > Copy auto-enables on text selection). Cross-platform bonus for the tablet half of the question: iPadOS menu bar menus "appear in the same order and with familiar sets of menu items" as Mac, and "Keyboard shortcuts in iPadOS use the same patterns as in macOS."

results.title: Windows — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for window management, resizing, and the multi-window/document model. Defines the two-type taxonomy a browser tab has no analogue for: a *primary* window (main navigation and content) vs an *auxiliary* window ("dedicated to one experience… doesn't allow navigation to other app areas, and it typically includes a button people use to close it"). Key rules: "Make sure that your windows adapt fluidly to different sizes to support multitasking and multiwindow workflows"; "Choose the right moment to open a new window" — Mail's Compose example, and the counterweight "opening new windows excessively creates clutter… Avoid opening new windows as default behavior"; "Consider providing the option to view content in a new window" via a context menu or the File menu; and the anti-Electron directive "Avoid creating custom window UI. System-provided windows look and behave in a way that people understand… Avoid making custom window frames or controls." Also covers iPadOS/visionOS windows, so it spans the tablet multitasking part of the question.

results.title: Designing for macOS — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The platform-characteristics overview that enumerates what makes desktop a distinct discipline from web: Display (large, high-resolution, extendable with additional displays including an iPad), Ergonomics (stationary use, 1–3 ft viewing distance — the reason desktop density differs from touch), Inputs ("any combination of input modes"), and App interactions ("People frequently have multiple apps open at the same time, and they expect smooth transitions between active and inactive states" — the active/inactive window state distinction browsers never model). Its prioritized directives are a compact checklist of exactly the omissions in the question: "Leverage large displays to present more content in fewer nested levels and with less need for modality"; "Let people resize, hide, show, and move your windows… and support full-screen mode"; "Use the menu bar to give people easy access to all the commands they need"; "Help people take advantage of high-precision input modes to perform pixel-perfect" selection.

results.title: Keyboards — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for keyboard shortcut conventions and the hybrid-input requirement. Defines a shortcut as "a combination of a primary key and one or more modifier keys (Control, Option, Shift, and Command)" and states "Apple defines standard keyboard shortcuts to work consistently across the system and most apps" with the rule "Respect standard keyboard shortcuts" — the Command-key convention that is where macOS and Windows (Control) diverge. Directly serves both halves of the question: covers physical keyboards on iPad ("iPad users often do" use one all the time) and the tablet-specific caveat that iPadOS apps should "avoid supporting keyboard navigation for controls, such as buttons, segmented controls, and switches" and route through Full Keyboard Access instead. "Support Full Keyboard Access when possible… lets people navigate and activate windows, menus, controls, and system features using only the keyboard" — available in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS.

results.title: Drag and drop — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Covers drag and drop between windows and between apps, which HTML5 drag-and-drop does not model semantically. States the move-vs-copy rule a web implementation must hand-code: "As a general rule, dropping selected content within the same container moves it, whereas dropping content in a different container copies it. Dragging and dropping content between apps always results in a copy." Enumerates the per-platform interaction differences (visionOS pinch-and-hold along the z-axis; iOS/iPadOS touch gestures, pointing device, and full keyboard-access mode; Universal Control letting people "drag content between their Mac and iPad"; macOS pointing device, full keyboard access, or VoiceOver). Two rules a web build usually skips: "As much as possible, support drag and drop throughout your app" (people "often try it everywhere"), and "Offer alternative ways to accomplish drag-and-drop actions" — menu commands plus accessibility APIs identifying sources and destinations.

results.title: Context menus — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Primary source for right-click/secondary-click menus, which web apps typically leave to the browser's own menu. Enumerates the reveal gestures per platform: "The system-defined touch or pinch and hold gesture in visionOS, iOS, and iPadOS; Pressing the Control key while clicking a pointing device in macOS and iPadOS; Using a secondary click on a Magic Trackpad in macOS or iPadOS." Constraints: "A context menu isn't for providing advanced or rarely used items"; "Aim for a small number of menu items"; "Support context menus consistently throughout your app" — inconsistency makes people "think there's a problem"; submenus "keep them to one level." The rule that ties back to the menu bar and matters most for discoverability: "Always make context menu items available in the main interface, too… In macOS, an app's menu bar menus list all the app's commands, including those in various context menus" — a hidden-by-default menu can never be the only path to a command.

claims.claim: Apple's iPadOS pointer system defines exactly three named content effects — highlight, lift, and hover — each with a prescribed use case: highlight for small elements with a transparent background, lift for small elements with an opaque background, and hover for large elements with customizable scale, tint, and shadow. The system applies highlight by default to bar buttons, tab bars, segmented controls, and edit menus, and lift by default to app icons and Control Center buttons.
claims.quote: iPadOS defines three content effects that bring focus to different types of interactive elements in your app: highlight, lift, and hover. […] By default, iPadOS applies the highlight effect to bar buttons, tab bars, segmented controls, and edit menus. […] By default, iPadOS applies the lift effect to app icons and to buttons in Control Center. […] Use highlight for a small element that has a transparent background. Use lift for a small element that has an opaque background. Use hover for large elements and customize the scale, tint, and shadow attributes as needed

claims.claim: Apple publishes specific numeric hit-region padding values for pointer targeting on iPadOS: approximately 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel, and approximately 24 points around the visible edges of elements without a bezel.
claims.quote: In general, it works well to add about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel; for elements without a bezel, it works well to add about 24 points of padding around the element’s visible edges.

claims.claim: Apple states that on iPad the pointing device is additive rather than substitutive — it does not replace touch — and requires that an app deliver an equivalent experience across gestures, pointer, and keyboard, meaning pointer-only interactions cannot be the sole path to a function.
claims.quote: On iPad and Apple Vision Pro, a pointing device gives people an additional way to interact with apps and content, without replacing touch, eyes, or gestures. […] The iPadOS pointing system gives people an additional way to interact with apps and content — it doesn’t replace touch. […] Provide a consistent experience in your app, whether people are using gestures, eyes, a pointing device, or a keyboard. People expect to move fluidly between multiple types of input, and they don’t want to learn different interactions for each mode or for each app they use.

claims.claim: Pointer magnetism in iPadOS is applied by default to elements using the lift and highlight effects but deliberately not to elements using the hover effect, because hover does not transform the default pointer shape and adding magnetism would feel jarring; magnetism also applies to text-entry areas.
claims.quote: By default, iPadOS applies magnetism to elements that use the lift effect (like app icons) and the highlight effect (like bar buttons), but not to elements that use hover. Because an element that supports hover doesn’t transform the default pointer shape, adding magnetism could be jarring and might make people feel that they’ve lost control of the pointer. The system also applies magnetism to text-entry areas

claims.claim: Apple sanctions using pointer proximity to reveal and hide auto-minimizing chrome (citing the iPadOS Safari toolbar and full-screen video playback controls), and separately requires that modifier-key behaviors produce identical results whether the user drags by touch or by pointer.
claims.quote: Let people use the pointer to reveal and hide controls that automatically minimize or fade out. In iPadOS, for example, people can reveal the minimized Safari toolbar by holding the pointer over it (the toolbar minimizes again when the pointer moves away). […] Provide a consistent experience when people press and hold a modifier key while interacting with objects in your app. For example, if people can duplicate an object by pressing and holding the Option key while they drag that object, ensure the result is the same whether they drag using touch or the pointer.

result.publishDate: No explicit publish date; page change log's most recent entry is June 21, 2023 ("Updated to include guidance for visionOS"). Retrieved 2026-08-01.

claims.claim: Android publishes five width window size classes with exact dp breakpoints — compact (<600dp), medium (600–839dp), expanded (840–1199dp), large (1200–1599dp), extra-large (≥1600dp) — plus three height classes: compact (<480dp), medium (480–899dp), expanded (≥900dp).
claims.quote: Compact width: width < 600dp (99.96% of phones in portrait) | Medium width: 600dp ≤ width < 840dp (93.73% of tablets in portrait) | Expanded width: 840dp ≤ width < 1200dp (97.22% of tablets in landscape) | Large width: 1200dp ≤ width < 1600dp (Large tablet displays) | Extra-large width: width ≥ 1600dp (Desktop displays) ... Compact height: height < 480dp | Medium height: 480dp ≤ height < 900dp | Expanded height: height ≥ 900dp

claims.claim: A window size class describes the app's window, not the physical device, so device-type ('isTablet') branching is explicitly wrong; split-screen, ChromeOS resizable windows, and foldables all decouple app window size from screen size.
claims.quote: Physical devices do not guarantee a specific window size class. The screen space available to your app can differ from the screen size of the device for many reasons. On mobile devices, split-screen mode can partition the screen between two applications. On ChromeOS, Android apps can be presented in desktop-type windows that are arbitrarily resizable. Foldables can have two different-sized screens individually accessed by folding or unfolding the device.

claims.claim: The window size class is dynamic and can change while the app is running due to orientation change, multitasking, or folding/unfolding, so the UI must adapt at runtime rather than being chosen once at launch.
claims.quote: The window size class can change throughout the lifetime of your app. While your app is running, device orientation changes, multitasking, and folding/unfolding can change the amount of screen space available. As a result, the window size class is dynamic, and your app's UI should adapt accordingly.

claims.claim: Width alone is insufficient: a phone or open flippable in landscape is typically medium width but compact height, a combination in which two-pane layouts are not practical — so height class must gate multi-pane decisions.
claims.quote: Most apps can build an adaptive UI by considering only the width window size class. However, also consider the height window size class for scenarios such as phones or open flippables in landscape orientation; the window width is typically medium, but window height is compact, in which case two pane layouts are not practical.

claims.claim: Size classes are intended for high-level layout decisions — specifically selecting a canonical layout (list-detail, supporting pane, feed) and adaptive navigation — and Google prescribes optimizing for expanded width first, then designing the medium-width case, testing at compact/medium/expanded breakpoints.
claims.quote: Use window size classes to make high-level application layout decisions, such as deciding whether to use a specific canonical layout to take advantage of additional screen space. ... As you make layout changes, test the layout behavior across all window sizes, especially at the compact, medium, and expanded breakpoint widths.

result.publishDate: 2026-06-16 (last updated, UTC)

claims.claim: Apple requires apps under Stage Manager to handle continuous, dynamic window resizing across a broad range of sizes — not a fixed set of layout states — using trait-collection observation or Auto Layout to adapt.
claims.quote: Respond to window resizing. Because people who use Stage Manager can dynamically resize their iPad app windows, your app's UI can transition through a broad range of sizes. Design your UI for flexible layout configurations, and make sure your app adapts to different window sizes quickly and smoothly.

claims.claim: Apple names the specific set of non-full-screen configurations an iPad app must be tested in: full screen, Split View, Slide Over, Picture in Picture, and dynamic resizing on an external display under Stage Manager.
claims.quote: Test your UI on different devices, in different environments. Consider the various configurations and sizes your UI can appear in, and make sure to test your app under those conditions. For example, test under the following conditions: full screen, Split View, Slide Over, Picture in Picture (PIP), and dynamic resizing in all dimensions while using Stage Manager with an external display.

claims.claim: Hybrid input on iPadOS requires the same UI element to present differently depending on whether input is touch or indirect (pointer/keyboard); Apple's edit menu API (UIEditMenuInteraction) exists specifically to change presentation style by input method.
claims.quote: A smooth text-editing experience takes advantage of standard system capabilities, and tailors itself according to touch or keyboard input. […] Create text-editing menus for the current input method. To create an edit menu that adjusts its presentation style according to touch or indirect input for an optimal user experience, see UIEditMenuInteraction.

claims.claim: Indirect input (trackpad/keyboard) on iPad is expected to support multi-selection without entering an explicit editing mode, and context menus should vary by whether zero, one, or many items are selected — interaction affordances a touch-only or web layout does not provide.
claims.quote: Enable lightweight multiple selection with indirect input. Allow people using indirect input methods, like a keyboard or trackpad, to select multiple items in a collection view without placing the collection view into editing mode. […] Specialize context menu options according to the number of selected items.

claims.claim: Apple provides an explicit desktop-density navigation style for iPad document apps (UINavigationItem.ItemStyle.editor) that relocates the title to the leading edge to free toolbar space, and when compiled with Mac Catalyst the navigation bar is automatically hosted by macOS's NSToolbar.
claims.quote: Navigation-based interfaces can use the editor style to bring the content density and flexibility of the Mac toolbar to iPad. This style moves the title to the leading side to open up more space for important controls […] By default, NSToolbar automatically hosts your navigation bar's content when its behavioral style is mac.

result.publishDate: No explicit publish/update date on the page; content is tied to WWDC22 sessions (10068, 10069, 10070, 10071, 10076, 110343), i.e. June 2022 / iPadOS 16 era, and has since been updated to reference visionOS compatibility.

claims.claim: Apple states that on iPadOS, designers should NOT build custom keyboard navigation for standard controls (buttons, segmented controls, switches) — Full Keyboard Access is the designated mechanism for control activation and gesture-based interactions like drag and drop; app-level keyboard navigation is scoped to text fields, text views, sidebars, and collection/custom views.
claims.quote: Although iPadOS supports keyboard navigation in text fields, text views, and sidebars, and provides APIs you can use to support it in collection views and other custom views, avoid supporting keyboard navigation for controls, such as buttons, segmented controls, and switches. Instead, let people use Full Keyboard Access to activate controls, navigate to all onscreen components, and perform gesture-based interactions like drag and drop.

claims.claim: Apple publishes a specific modifier-key hierarchy for custom macOS/iPadOS shortcuts: Command is the primary modifier, Shift is the secondary complement, Option is for less-common/power commands, and Control should be avoided because the system reserves it — a convention that inverts Windows practice where Ctrl is the primary modifier.
claims.quote: Command | ⌘ | Prefer the Command key as the main modifier key in a custom keyboard shortcut … Control | ⌃ | Avoid using the Control key as a modifier. The system uses Control in many systemwide features and shortcuts

claims.claim: Apple mandates a fixed display order for multi-modifier shortcuts — Control, Option, Shift, Command — a typographic convention with no web equivalent.
claims.quote: List modifier keys in the correct order. If you use more than one modifier key in a custom shortcut, always list them in this order: Control, Option, Shift, Command.

claims.claim: Apple treats a physical keyboard as an expected input on iPad, not an edge case: hardware keyboards are supported on every Apple device except Apple Watch, and Apple explicitly says iPad users often use one — establishing hybrid touch/keyboard input as a baseline iPadOS design requirement.
claims.quote: People can connect a physical keyboard to any device except Apple Watch. Mac users tend to use a physical keyboard all the time and iPad users often do.

claims.claim: Apple prohibits repurposing standard system keyboard shortcuts for custom actions, permitting redefinition only when the standard action has no meaning in the app (e.g. reusing Command-I in an app with no text editing).
claims.quote: In general, don't repurpose standard keyboard shortcuts for custom actions. People can get confused when the shortcuts they know work differently in your app or game. Only consider redefining a standard shortcut if its action doesn't make sense in your experience.

result.publishDate: Last updated June 9, 2025 (changelog: \"Moved game-specific key bindings guidance to the Game controls page.\"); prior entries June 10, 2024 and June 21, 2023

claims.claim: Apple's iPadOS HIG requires apps to adapt to multitasking modes as a first-class appearance change, alongside orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type — i.e. an iPad app must not assume it owns a fixed full-screen canvas, and must also survive transition to running under macOS.
claims.quote: Adapt seamlessly to appearance changes — like device orientation, multitasking modes, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type — and transition effortlessly to running in macOS, letting people choose the configurations that work best for them.

claims.claim: Apple states that iPad users combine multiple simultaneous input modes — Multi-Touch gestures, virtual keyboards, an attached physical keyboard or pointing device, Apple Pencil, and voice — so hybrid input is the documented default assumption on iPadOS, not an edge case.
claims.quote: Inputs. People can interact with iPad using Multi-Touch gestures and virtual keyboards, an attached keyboard or pointing device, Apple Pencil, or voice, and they often combine multiple input modes.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly directs designers to support combined-input interactions rather than designing for one input mode at a time.
claims.quote: Let people use Multi-Touch gestures, a physical keyboard or trackpad, or Apple Pencil, and consider supporting unique interactions that combine multiple input modes.

claims.claim: Apple's stated large-display guidance for iPad is to minimize modal interfaces and full-screen transitions — the opposite of the phone-derived pattern of pushing full-screen views — and to place controls within reach but out of the way.
claims.quote: Take advantage of the large display to elevate the content people care about, minimizing modal interfaces and full-screen transitions, and positioning onscreen controls where they’re easy to reach, but not in the way.

claims.claim: Apple specifies a concrete iPad ergonomic parameter — users are typically within about 3 feet of the device — and instructs designers to derive onscreen content size and density from viewing distance plus input mode, which is why phone metrics do not transfer directly. The page also names multi-app onscreen use and inter-app drag and drop as core iPadOS expectations.
claims.quote: people are typically within about 3 feet of the device as they interact with it

result.publishDate: No explicit publish or revision date on the page. Content is current-generation: it links WWDC 2025 sessions "Meet Liquid Glass", "Get to know the new design system", and "Elevate the design of your iPad app", so it reflects the iPadOS 26-era HIG (2025 or later).

claims.claim: Apple's current iPadOS layout guidance frames multitasking as macOS-style free window resizing rather than the older fixed Split View / Slide Over modes: windows resize continuously down to a minimum width and height, and designers must account for the full range of possible window sizes. Notably, the page never names Split View, Slide Over, or Stage Manager anywhere in its iPadOS section.
claims.quote: People can freely resize windows down to a minimum width and height, similar to window behavior in macOS. It’s important to account for this resizing behavior and the full range of possible window sizes when designing your layout.

claims.claim: Apple prescribes a specific collapse order for adaptive layouts: design the full-screen layout first, defer switching to a compact view as long as possible, and for multi-column layouts hide tertiary columns (such as inspectors) before collapsing further.
claims.quote: As someone resizes a window, defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible. Design for a full-screen view first, and only switch to a compact view when a version of the full layout no longer fits. This helps the UI feel more stable and familiar in as many situations as possible. For more complex layouts such as [split views], prefer hiding tertiary columns such as inspectors as the view narrows.

claims.claim: Apple names the concrete iPad window sizes a designer must test against — halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen produced by the system window controls — rather than publishing CSS-style pixel breakpoints.
claims.quote: Test your layout at common system-provided sizes, and provide smooth transitions. Window controls provide the option to arrange windows to fill halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen, so it’s important to check your layout at each of these sizes on a variety of devices. Be sure to minimize unexpected UI changes as people adjust down to the minimum and up to the maximum window size.

claims.claim: Apple's size class system is binary (regular or compact) per axis, not a numeric breakpoint ladder; the accompanying specification table lists every iPad model — Pro 12.9-inch, Pro 11-inch, Pro 10.5-inch, Air 13-inch, Air 11-inch, iPad 11-inch, iPad 9.7-inch, iPad mini 7.9-inch — as 'Regular width, regular height' in BOTH portrait and landscape, whereas iPhones vary by orientation (e.g. iPhone 17 Pro Max: compact width/regular height portrait, regular width/compact height landscape).
claims.quote: A size class is a value that’s either regular or compact, where regular refers to a larger screen or a screen in landscape orientation and compact refers to a smaller screen or a screen in portrait orientation. […] Different size class combinations apply to the full-screen experience on different devices, based on screen size.

claims.claim: Apple's macOS layout guidance imposes a window-management constraint absent from web design: controls and critical information must not sit at the bottom of a window, because users routinely drag windows so the bottom edge falls off-screen.
claims.quote: Avoid placing controls or critical information at the bottom of a window. People often move windows so that the bottom edge is below the bottom of the screen.

result.publishDate: Last updated September 9, 2025 (per the page's own change log; prior substantive revisions June 9, 2025 "Added guidance for Liquid Glass" and February 2, 2024 "Enhanced guidance for avoiding system controls in iPadOS app layouts")

claims.claim: Material Design 3 has renamed "window size classes" to "breakpoints", and the assigned URL (/foundations/layout/applying-layout/window-size-classes) now returns HTTP 404 — the live primary page is https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/breakpoints/overview. M3 states these breakpoints apply to both Android and web.
claims.quote: A breakpoint (previously window size class) is the window size at which a layout needs to change to match available space, device conventions, and ergonomics. These apply to Android and web.

claims.claim: Material defines five width breakpoints with exact dp values: Compact under 600dp (phone portrait), Medium 600–839dp (tablet portrait, unfolded foldable portrait), Expanded 840–1199dp (phone landscape, tablet landscape, desktop), Large 1200–1599dp (desktop), Extra-large 1600dp+ (desktop, ultra-wide monitors). Note these differ from the older three-class compact/medium/expanded system where expanded was 840dp+ with no upper bound.
claims.quote: Breakpoint Width (dp) Common devices — Compact Under 600dp Phone in portrait; Medium 600–839dp Tablet in portrait, Foldable in portrait (unfolded); Expanded 840–1199dp Phone in landscape, Tablet in landscape, Foldable in landscape (unfolded), Desktop; Large 1200–1599dp Desktop; Extra-large 1600dp+ Desktop, Ultra-wide monitors

claims.claim: Pane count is prescribed per breakpoint: one pane for compact and medium, two recommended for expanded and large, up to three for extra-large. M3 additionally warns against two panes at medium when content is information-dense — which means a tablet in portrait (600–839dp) is a single-pane target, not automatically a split view.
claims.quote: Compact and medium breakpoints: A single pane works best. Expanded and large breakpoints: Two panes are recommended. Extra-large breakpoints: Consider using three panes… Don’t use two panes in medium layouts with high information density, as it can reduce usability.

claims.claim: Material prescribes swapping the navigation component by breakpoint rather than scaling it: navigation bar at compact, collapsed navigation rail at medium and expanded, and modal or standard expanded navigation rail at large and extra-large.
claims.quote: Swap a navigation bar in a compact layout for a navigation rail in a medium or expanded layout… A collapsed navigation rail in medium or expanded layouts can become an expanded navigation rail in large or extra-large layouts

claims.claim: M3 explicitly rejects the stretched-phone-layout approach, framing adaptation as five decisions — reveal, divide, resize, reposition, swap — and states that extra space must not simply enlarge the same UI; it also caps line length at 40–60 characters across all breakpoints.
claims.quote: Additional space doesn’t just mean making the same thing bigger… Start by designing for one breakpoint, then adjust the layout for the next size by asking these five questions… Across all breakpoints, adjust margins and type styles to keep text between 40–60 characters per line.

claims.claim: Google publishes three named canonical layouts — list-detail, feed, and supporting pane — as the prescribed large-screen alternatives to a single stretched layout, derived from Material Design and backed by framework components.
claims.quote: Canonical layouts are proven, versatile layouts that provide an optimal user experience on a variety of form factors. […] The canonical layouts support small screen phones as well as tablets, foldables, and ChromeOS devices. Derived from Material Design guidance, the layouts are aesthetic as well as functional.

claims.claim: Android's window size class width breakpoints are numerically specified as compact < 600dp, medium >= 600dp, and expanded >= 840dp, and layout resources are keyed to them via layout, layout-w600dp, and layout-w840dp folders.
claims.quote: Establish the window size classes that divide the amount of horizontal display space available for your app into three categories: compact (< 600dp), medium (>= 600dp), and expanded (>= 840dp).

claims.claim: The list-detail layout changes pane visibility by width class: expanded width shows list and detail simultaneously, while medium and compact widths show only one at a time with back navigation returning to the list.
claims.quote: Expanded-width displays accommodate both the list and detail at the same time. Selection of a list item updates the detail pane to show the related content for the selected item. […] Medium- and compact-width displays show either the list or the detail, depending on user interaction with the app. When just the list is visible, selection of a list item displays the detail in place of the list. When just the detail is visible, pressing the back button redisplays the list.

claims.claim: Google requires apps to preserve state and pane content across runtime window size class changes (rotation or app window resizing, i.e. multitasking/resizable windows), specifying exactly which pane survives each transition.
claims.quote: Configuration changes such as device orientation changes or app window size changes can change the display's window size class. A list‑detail layout responds accordingly, preserving app state: - If an expanded-width display showing both the list and detail panes narrows to medium or compact, the detail pane remains visible and the list pane is hidden

claims.claim: The supporting pane layout has a prescribed proportional split that differs by size class: equal horizontal split at medium width, but 30% supporting / 70% main at expanded width.
claims.quote: Medium: In the `layout-w600dp` folder, provide supporting pane content that results in the main content and supporting pane rendering side by side, splitting the horizontal display space equally - Expanded: In the `layout-w840dp` folder, include supporting pane content that results in the main content and supporting pane rendering side by side; however, the supporting pane takes up only 30% of the horizontal space, leaving the remaining 70% for the main content

result.publishDate: 2026-06-16 (last updated)

claims.claim: Material Design 3 gates the navigation rail on window size class: it is only for medium breakpoints and larger, and compact windows must use a navigation bar instead. This is the primary-source basis for 'don't stretch the phone layout' on tablets.
claims.quote: Only use navigation rails for medium breakpoints and larger. Don't use a navigation bar. ... Compact: Don't use a standard navigation rail for compact layouts due to space constraints. Use a navigation bar instead.

claims.claim: The page publishes the concrete dp values for Material's window size classes inline: compact is under 600dp, medium is 600dp to 839dp (tablet or foldable in portrait), and extra-large is 1600dp and larger.
claims.quote: medium Window widths from 600dp to 839dp, such as a tablet or foldable in portrait orientation ... extra large breakpoints Window widths 1600dp and larger, such as ultra-wide monitors ... Compact windows Window widths smaller than 600dp, such as a phone in portrait orientation

claims.claim: The rail and the bottom navigation bar are mutually exclusive, not additive: the rail transforms into a bar when the window shrinks, and showing both at once is explicitly prohibited.
claims.quote: When moving from a large screen to a small screen, a navigation rail can transform into a navigation bar, providing the same quick access in a configuration that's easier to use on smaller displays. Never use the navigation rail and navigation bar simultaneously.

claims.claim: Destination-count rules are specified: the collapsed rail holds 3-7 items and must not be hidden, and at expanded/extra-large sizes with more than five destinations Material directs designers to a modal expanded rail. It also says medium windows with few destinations may be better served by a navigation bar.
claims.quote: The collapsed nav rail runs along the leading edge of the window, and should contain 3-7 navigation items. It should not be hidden. ... If there are more than five destinations, consider using a modal expanded nav rail instead. ... In medium windows with few destinations, consider using a navigation bar instead.

claims.claim: Placement is constrained by the adaptive layout system rather than free-form: the rail sits outside any pane, on the window's leading edge, never inside body content, never horizontal; and on tablets specifically its items should be center-aligned for reachability.
claims.quote: In adaptive layouts, the navigation rail should be placed outside any panes, always along the leading edge of the window. Don't place it within body content. ... On tablets, use center alignment to make it easier to reach items.

result.publishDate: Not stated — m3.material.io is an undated living spec; page retrieved 2026-08-01 (Material Design 3 expressive-era content, references the "expressive update")

claims.claim: Google's Adaptive app quality guidelines define three named tiers, with Tier 3 ("Adaptive ready") as the floor: the app must fill the entire screen or window, must not be letterboxed or run in compatibility mode, and must provide basic support for keyboard, mouse, trackpad, and stylus — i.e. large-screen support is graded, not binary.
claims.quote: TIER 3 (basic) — Adaptive ready: Your app runs full screen (or full window in multi-window mode) on all devices, but app layout might not be ideal. The app is not letterboxed; it does not run in compatibility mode. Users can complete critical task flows but with a less than optimal user experience. The app provides basic support for external input devices, including keyboard, mouse, trackpad, and stylus.

claims.claim: Tier 2 ("Adaptive optimized") requires that adaptive layout implementation be driven by window size classes and that multi-pane canonical layouts be used on large screens, naming ListDetailPaneScaffold for Compose and Activity embedding for legacy view apps as the sanctioned mechanisms.
claims.quote: App has responsive and adaptive layouts designed for all screen sizes. All layouts are responsive... Implementation of adaptive layouts is determined by window size classes. ... Create multi-pane layouts (where appropriate) to take advantage of large screen space. See Canonical layouts. For Jetpack Compose apps, use adaptive layouts (such as ListDetailPaneScaffold) to build multi-pane UIs. For legacy activity-based apps, Activity embedding enables multi-pane layouts by displaying activities side by side.

claims.claim: Google explicitly enumerates the failure modes of a stretched phone layout as testable defects (requirement UI_Secondary_Elements, test T-Layout_Flow): full-width bottom sheets, buttons, and text fields on large screens are non-compliant, and navigation bars must be replaced by navigation rails while navigation drawers become expanded rails.
claims.quote: Bottom sheets are not full width on large screens (apply maximum width); Buttons are not full width on large screens; Text fields and boxes don't stretch to full width on large screens; Small edit menus or modals don't cover the entire screen; Context menus appear next to the selected item; Navigation rails replace navigation bars for better ergonomics on large screens; Navigation drawers are updated to expanded navigation rails

claims.claim: Tier 2 makes hybrid input a hard requirement set with individual test IDs: hover states on actionable elements (T-Hover_States), right-click/secondary-tap context menus (T-Context_Menus), Tab and arrow-key navigation (T-Keyboard_Navigation), and keyboard shortcuts for select/cut/copy/paste/undo/redo (T-Keyboard_Shortcuts), plus Esc-to-exit and Spacebar-to-play semantics.
claims.quote: Actionable UI elements have hover states (where appropriate) to indicate to mouse and trackpad users that the elements are interactive. ... Context menus are accessible by typical mouse and trackpad right-click (secondary mouse button or secondary tap) behavior. ... App supports keyboard shortcuts for commonly used actions: Select, Cut, Copy, Paste, Undo, Redo

claims.claim: Even at the basic Tier 3 level, an Android app must remain fully functional when it does not own the full screen: multi-window functionality is required, and multi-resume requires the app to keep updating its UI while it is not the top-focused app and to handle loss of exclusive resources such as camera and microphone.
claims.quote: App is fully functional in multi-window mode. ... App fully supports multi-resume. App updates its UI (continues playing media, incorporates new messages, updates download progress, etc.) when the app is not the top focused app. In addition, the app handles the loss of exclusive resources such as cameras and microphones in multi-window scenarios.

claims.claim: Apple prescribes a fixed menu-bar order for macOS and iPadOS apps — app name, File, Edit, Format, View, app-specific menus, Window, Help — with the Apple menu pinned to the leading side and menu bar extras to the trailing side on macOS; adopting the system-defined menus and their ordering is a requirement, not a suggestion.
claims.quote: When present in the menu bar, the following menus appear in the order listed below. YourAppName (you supply a short version of your app's name for this menu's title) / File / Edit / Format / View / App-specific menus, if any / Window / Help ... Support the default system-defined menus and their ordering. People expect to find menus and menu items in an order they're familiar with.

claims.claim: Menu items must remain visible at all times and be disabled when unavailable — hiding inapplicable commands is explicitly disallowed, the opposite of the common web pattern of conditionally rendering unavailable actions out of the DOM.
claims.quote: Always show the same set of menu items. Keeping menu items visible helps people learn what actions your app supports, even if they're unavailable in the current context. If a menu bar item isn't actionable, disable the action instead of hiding it from the menu.

claims.claim: Every app command must be listed in the menu bar even when it is reachable elsewhere in the UI; Apple states that omitting commands — including infrequently used or advanced ones — breaks discoverability, keyboard-shortcut assignment, and Full Keyboard Access accessibility. This is a duplication requirement a browser-based design has no equivalent of.
claims.quote: Even when commands are available elsewhere in your app, it's important to list them in the menu bar. Putting commands in the menu bar makes them easier for people to find, lets you assign keyboard shortcuts to them, and makes them more accessible to people using Full Keyboard Access. Excluding commands from the menu bar — even infrequently used or advanced commands — risks making them difficult for everyone to find.

claims.claim: A Window menu containing Minimize and Zoom is required even for single-window apps, specifically so Full Keyboard Access users can invoke window management from the keyboard; Apple separates window appearance (View menu) from window navigation/management (Window menu) and from closing (File menu).
claims.quote: Provide a Window menu even if your app has only one window. Include the Minimize and Zoom menu items so people using Full Keyboard Access can use the keyboard to invoke these functions.

claims.claim: On iPadOS the menu bar is hidden until revealed (vs. always visible on macOS), is centered rather than leading-aligned, has no Apple menu and no menu bar extras, and shows window controls when the app is full screen — and because it is often hidden and because modifier-key dynamic items require a hardware keyboard, every menu-bar function must also be reachable from the app's own UI.
claims.quote: Because the menu bar is often hidden when running an app full screen, ensure that people can access all of your app's functions through its UI. In particular, always offer other ways to accomplish tasks assigned to dynamic menu items, since these are only available when a hardware keyboard is connected. Avoid using the menu bar as a catch-all location for functionality that doesn't fit in elsewhere.

result.publishDate: Last updated June 9, 2025 (change log: "Added guidance for the menu bar in iPadOS"; page metadata alert-date 2025-06-09). No original publish date given.

claims.claim: Apple's HIG explicitly instructs designers to prefer split views in a regular (not compact) horizontal size class environment, because a compact environment — iPhone in portrait is the named example — cannot display multiple panes without wrapping or truncating content. This is Apple's primary-source statement of why a phone-width layout and a multi-pane tablet layout are different design problems, keyed to size classes.
claims.quote: **Prefer using a split view in a regular — not a compact — environment.** A split view needs horizontal space in which to display multiple panes. In a compact environment, such as iPhone in portrait orientation, it's difficult to display multiple panes without wrapping or truncating the content, making it less legible and harder to interact with.

claims.claim: On iPadOS, Apple's split view supports either two vertical panes (Mail) or three vertical panes (Keynote), and the named implementations are SwiftUI's NavigationSplitView and UIKit's UISplitViewController. This confirms the two-column and three-column split-view pattern as Apple's canonical large-screen layout, with the specific API names.
claims.quote: In iPadOS, a split view can include either two vertical panes, like Mail, or three vertical panes, like Keynote.

claims.claim: Apple requires iPadOS split-view layouts to be designed for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths — not just full screen — because iPad windows are fluidly resizable, and requires that navigating between panes remain logical at every width. This is the primary-source obligation a designer must meet when the app does not own the full screen (multitasking / resizable windows).
claims.quote: **Account for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths.** Since iPad windows are fluidly resizable, it's important to consider the design of a split view layout at multiple widths. In particular, ensure that it's possible to navigate between the various panes in a logical way.

claims.claim: For macOS, Apple specifies desktop-only pane behavior absent from web layout: panes can be arranged vertically, horizontally, or both; dividers are draggable to resize; the preferred thin divider style measures exactly one point in width; and apps must set reasonable minimum and maximum pane sizes so the divider stays visible.
claims.quote: **Prefer the thin divider style.** The thin divider measures one point in width, giving you maximum space for content while remaining easy for people to use.

The imperative in the same sentence is "Let people use" — i.e. support each input mode. Rendering "consider supporting" as "explicitly directs" upgrades an optional suggestion into a directive the page does not issue.

(2) Substantive inversion — the "rather than" is a false dichotomy Apple contradicts. Apple's Pointing devices HIG (developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices) states outright: "The iPadOS pointing system gives people an additional way to interact with apps and content — it doesn't replace touch," and "On iPad and Apple Vision Pro, a pointing device gives people an additional way to interact with apps and content, without replacing touch, eyes, or gestures," plus a parity requirement: "ensure the result is the same whether they drag using touch or the pointer." Touchscreen gestures HIG likewise says "Avoid requiring specific body movements or positions for input" and "consider supporting alternative inputs to let people choose the interaction method that works best for them." Apple Pencil HIG: "it's essential to avoid requiring people to tap a button or enter a special mode before they can make a mark." So Apple's actual direction is per-mode parity — every mode fully functional independently — with combined-mode interactions as an additive bonus. The claim's "rather than designing for one input mode at a time" reverses the priority Apple states.

A supportable restatement would be: "Apple observes that iPad users often combine multiple input modes, and suggests designers consider interactions that combine them — while requiring that each input mode remain independently sufficient." The claim as written is not that.
